title: From RNNs to Transformers and BERT
oneLiner: How models learned to read whole sentences: step-by-step memory networks, then attention that looks back at every word, then Transformers and BERT.

what.html:
Early neural translators read a sentence word by word into one summary, then wrote the translation from it. Long sentences didn't fit. Attention let the writer look back at every input word. Transformers went further: every word looks at every other word at once, in parallel. BERT is a Transformer trained to fill in hidden words, giving each word a meaning that depends on its sentence.

Everyday versionSummarising a whole book on a postcard loses details; keeping the book open and glancing back at the right page while you write doesn't.

why.html:
• This is the architecture inside today's chatbots and search engines.
  • It explains why long sentences used to be hard and why they aren't now.
  • "Pre-train once, fine-tune for many tasks" started here.

how.title: Read, summarise, write
how.html: "I love you" isn't "Je aime tu"; it's "Je t'aime". An encoder reads the whole sentence into a summary and a decoder writes the translation. But the summary has a fixed size.

how.title: A running memory
how.html: A recurrent network updates its memory with each word, like adding drops of colour to water. For "I don't like NLP", the memory goes [0.76, 0] → [0.36, −0.76] → …

how.title: Fading signals, and a fix
how.html: Learning signals shrink each step back in time, so early words are forgotten. LSTMs add a protected "conveyor belt" memory with gates deciding what to keep, add and show.

how.title: Look back where it matters
how.html: At each output word, score every input word, turn scores into percentages and mix: 73% "bank", 27% "river".

how.title: Every word looks at every word
how.html: In a Transformer, each word asks a question (query), advertises itself (key) and offers content (value). "it" attends to "animal" when the sentence ends "tired", and to "street" when it ends "wide".

how.title: Many heads, masks and shortcuts
how.html: Several attention "heads" look for different things. Masks hide padding and, when generating, the future. Shortcut connections and normalisation keep deep stacks trainable.

how.title: Where is each word?
how.html: Attention alone ignores word order, so each position gets a unique wave pattern added to its word vector, like clock hands at different speeds.

how.title: BERT
how.html: Hide 15% of the words and learn to guess them from both sides ("The [MASK] sat on the [MASK]"). The result: "bank" gets a river-ish or money-ish meaning depending on its sentence, and a small extra layer adapts BERT to almost any task.

demo.html: Compare how many steps must happen one after another in an RNN and a Transformer, and what the Transformer pays instead: comparing every pair of words.

example.html:
An attention step. The decoder state [1, 0] scores "bank" [1, 1] as 1 and "river" [0, 1] as 0. Softmax gives 0.73 and 0.27, so the context vector is 0.73 × [1, 1] + 0.27 × [0, 1] = [0.73, 1.00].

Supplementary While training a translator, the decoder is fed the correct previous word rather than its own guess ("teacher forcing"), which speeds learning.

misunderstandings: Transformers read left to right like RNNs.
Encoders see all positions at once.
BERT generates text like a chatbot.
It's an encoder for understanding tasks.
Positional encodings are learned word meanings.
takeaways: Encoder–decoder with one fixed vector = bottleneck.
RNN: hₜ = tanh(W_h hₜ₋₁ + W_x xₜ); gradients vanish; LSTMs help.
Transformer: softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V, multi-head, masks, residual + LayerNorm, positional encodings.
BERT: bidirectional encoder, MLM (15%), NSP, fine-tuning.
thirty: Seq2seq encoders compress the source into a fixed context vector (bottleneck); word-for-word fails (Je t'aime). RNNs update hₜ = tanh(W_h hₜ₋₁ + W_x xₜ + b): for 'I don't like NLP', h₁ = [0.762, 0], h₂ = [0.363, −0.762]. Gradients multiply per step and vanish; LSTMs add a gated cell (Cₜ = fC + iC̃). Attention scores encoder states against the decoder state, softmaxes and mixes: s = [1, 0], bank [1, 1], river [0, 1] → 0.73/0.27, c = [0.73, 1.00]. Transformers use self-attention softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V in parallel, multi-head with W^O, feed-forward 512→2048→512, padding and look-ahead masks, residual + LayerNorm, and sinusoidal positional encodings. BERT stacks encoders, pre-trains with masked LM (15%: 80/10/10) and NSP, gives contextual embeddings (river vs money bank), and is fine-tuned with small heads.

opts: A fixed-size context vector for any input length
